newsitem.title: CANADA: Suncor unveils major oil sands expansion.
newsitem.headline: Suncor unveils major oil sands expansion.

text.p: Suncor Energy Inc. unveiled plans Thursday to invest C$2.2 billion ($1.6 billion) in its Alberta oil sands business to boost synthetic crude oil output to 210,000 barrels a day by 2002.
Suncor said the programme, called Project Millenium, would expand oil sands extraction and upgrading facilities and increase production to almost 250 percent from current levels.
The investment was in addition to C$600 million ($438 million) of expansion projects under way at Suncor's oil sands facility in Fort McMurray in northeastern Alberta.
Previous initiatives were expected to bring production to 105,000 barrels a day by 1999. Suncor's oil sands business now produces about 85,000 barrels a day.

The announcement sent Calgary-based Suncor's stock soaring Thursday. Its shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange jumped C$4.05 to C$42.50. The company's New York Stock Exchange-listed shares were up $3.8125 to $31.75 in midday trading.

Canada's oil sands industry -- which mines the heavy oil or bitumen, separates petroleum from the sand then upgrades it into light oil -- is already the target of billions of dollars worth of expansions and new projects over the next five years.
Oil from oil sands currently makes up about 20 percent of Canadian demand.

Suncor Chief Executive Rick George said in a statement that the major investment was expected to generate a return on capital greater than 15 percent -- "more than double the average rate of return for the Canadian conventional oil and gas sector."

The first phase of Project Millennium was a C$190 million ($139 million) investment in the existing plant. That work, which would begin immediately, would gradually increase production to 130,000 barrels a day by 2001, said Suncor, whose current operation is second in size after Syncrude Canada Ltd.
The second phase would be led off by a C$90 million ($66 million) technical, environmental and socioeconomic assessment to determine the best approach to the expansion.
When the study is complete, Suncor's board will make a final decision on the configuration of the full expansion and construction would start in 1999, the company said.
Suncor said that as its oil sands production rose, economies of scale and technological and reliability improvements would send costs per barrel to new lows.
"When the 210,000 barrel-per-day target is reached in 2002, Suncor estimates its cash costs will be C$10 ($7.30) to C$11 ($8.03) per barrel, compared with C$15 ($10.95) per barrel today.," it said.
At this cost, products would be fully competitive with most sources of crude in North America, Suncor said.

In other oil sands news Thursday, Shell Canada Ltd. announced a proposal to build a C$375 million ($274 million) pipeline that would ship bitumen to Edmonton, Alberta, from its planned C$1 billion ($730 million) oil sands project near Fort McMurray.
The pipeline, which would tie into Shell Canada's Scotford Refinery, would be in operation in 2002, the same time frame as the proposed Sucnor oil sands project.
